analysis.one_liner: Repeals the excise tax on chemicals that funds toxic waste site cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Superfund chemical tax was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on January 22, 2025, and has had no further action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law charges chemical makers and importers a per-ton tax (roughly 44 cents to $9.74 per ton) on 42 listed chemicals and 151 chemical substances, with the money going into the Superfund that pays for cleaning up contaminated sites. This bill eliminates that tax, retroactive to January 1, 2024, removing a dedicated funding stream for hazardous waste cleanup.
analysis.who_benefits: Chemical manufacturers and importers, who would stop paying the per-ton tax and could claim refunds for taxes paid since the start of 2024 under the retroactive effective date.

how_it_helps.text: Removes an excise tax of 44 cents to $9.74 per ton on taxable chemicals manufactured in or imported into the United States, which runs through the end of 2031 under current law.
Makes the repeal retroactive to January 1, 2024, meaning companies that already paid the tax could recover payments for roughly the first year it was in force.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary taxpayers and communities near contaminated sites. The tax revenue goes into the Hazardous Substance Superfund, which pays to remediate polluted sites; without it, cleanup funding would have to come from general tax revenue or the sites would sit uncleaned longer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

drawbacks.text: Repealing the tax eliminates revenue deposited into the Superfund, which finances the remediation of environmentally contaminated sites, shifting that cost to general taxpayers or leaving sites uncleaned.
The retroactive effective date means the federal government would owe refunds on taxes already collected in 2024 and 2025, deepening the revenue loss.

A fair objection in the bill's favor: the tax raises input costs for domestic manufacturers and can be passed through to prices, though the tax applies to imported chemicals as well as domestically produced ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, targeted benefit to the chemical industry while removing a dedicated 'polluter pays' funding stream for cleaning up hazardous waste sites. The savings to manufacturers would be paid for through general tax revenue or unremediated sites, so the cost lands broadly on the public rather than on the companies whose chemicals are associated with contamination.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Beth Van Duyne introduced the Chemical Tax Repeal Act on January 22, 2025, with Reps. Carey, LaHood, and Miller of West Virginia joining as original sponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day and has had no further action.
Nine House Republicans have cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors are Republicans.
The bill would strike the subchapters of the tax code imposing the chemical excise taxes and make the repeal effective January 1, 2024.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained because the bill has not advanced; the Superfund chemical tax remains in force, and the chemical industry is better off than it would be if the repeal were moving toward passage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical makers, if it ever passes

for.name: Rep. Beth Van Duyne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Superfund chemical excise tax.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors are House Republicans, and there is no record of any Democrat supporting it; no member has acted against it because it has not come to a vote.

industries.note: The bill ends a per-ton excise tax on 42 listed chemicals and 151 chemical substances, retroactive to the start of 2024. The tax is the dedicated funding source for Superfund cleanup of contaminated sites, so the industry's savings come directly out of a fund meant to make polluters pay for remediation.

industries.industry: Superfund cleanup program and communities near contaminated sites
industries.note: Repealing the tax cuts off revenue deposited into the Hazardous Substance Superfund, which pays to remediate environmentally contaminated sites. Cleanup would depend on general taxpayer money or proceed more slowly.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has a small all-Republican cosponsor list and has sat untouched in Ways and Means since January 2025. Revenue-losing tax bills in this position rarely reach the floor, and with divided control of Congress any repeal of a dedicated cleanup tax would also face Senate resistance, so it is unlikely to advance in this Congress.
